title: Commit parallel batches in order

blocks.text: An import splits a file into numbered batches and processes them on a pool of workers, in parallel. The batches must still be committed to the database in batch order, because each one continues the running totals of the one before. A worker that has finished batch `n` calls `awaitTurn(n)`, commits, and calls `done(n)`.

Since the sequencer went in, two things have shown up in the logs: a batch committed while the batch before it was still committing, and, on another day, an import that stopped with every worker idle and a finished batch waiting for a turn that had already come.

Write `awaitTurn(...)` and `done(...)` in `src/main/java/practice/CommitSequencer.java`, on the monitor of its `lock` field. A worker waits without using the processor until its batch's turn, and whatever order the workers start waiting in, each batch goes ahead exactly when the one before it is done. About eight lines in total.

cases.says: a batch whose turn it is goes ahead at once, and done passes the turn to the next batch
a batch that waits for its turn goes ahead once the batch before it is done
when the turn passes to one batch, a later batch that is also waiting keeps waiting
when the turn passes, the batch whose turn it is goes ahead even if a later batch started waiting first

origin.section: wait() Belongs in a Loop Over Its Condition, and a Change Is Announced With notifyAll()

concepts: notify() wakes one arbitrary waiter, which may not be able to use the change; notifyAll() wakes every waiter to re-check.
A return from wait() doesn't mean the condition holds; wait() is called in a loop that re-checks it.
